reasoning: The sink is real. At ZAIWireTypes.swift:83-84, `.map { Int($0) }` runs on a Double from flexibleDoubleIfPresent (AppConfig.swift:199-203), and nothing checks range or finiteness first. So a value like 1e19 would crash the app instead of throwing an error. Nothing in the decode path stops that crash. What does not hold is the attacker-controlled source. The only input is the response from a hard-coded HTTPS endpoint: ZAIProvider.swift:10 `private static let usageURL = URL(string: "https://api.z.ai/api/monitor/usage/quota/limit")!`, used unchanged at ZAIProvider.swift:44. The Z.AI config has no user-set base_url, so the request cannot be redirected to a host the attacker runs. The system's default TLS handling (ATS) blocks a third party from changing the body in transit. The only party that can shape this JSON is the vendor itself, which is already trusted with the user's API key and with the data the app shows, or someone who has already broken TLS. The finding's precondition, 'attacker controls or influences the Z.AI API response', takes that control for granted and never shows it. The poisoned DiskCache also cannot be reached independently, because it only ever stores this same trusted payload. So the fixed host plus TLS is an effective defense against an outside attacker, and item 1 of the proof standard (a source the attacker controls) fails. Separate note: this is still worth fixing as a robustness bug. Switching to `Int(exactly:)` after rounding, or checking the range first, would stop a malformed vendor response from crashing the app. It is not a vulnerability as the finding describes it.
